title.en: A Personal Note from Rabbi Feigenbaum for Parents, Mechanchim, and Mechanchos

spans.text:
A Personal Note
A PERSONAL NOTE  
FROM RABBI FEIGENBAUM FOR 
PARENTS, MECHANCHIM, AND 
MECHANCHOS
Teens—see page 240 for YOUR personal note! 
“Are you sure my kid/student should be reading this? I grew up fine without all this stuff!”Me too! I went to school in the ’50s and ’60s, and I don’t remember asking any of these questions! In addition, as you are well aware, today there are a plethora of books on the overall topic of
— how to approach it, if to approach it, intellectual analysis, appeals to the emotions, self-awareness, new-age and old-age, and so on! In addition, there are many books and
that deal with very specific issues of Torah

, and many of these works are heavily footnoted, showing a level of erudition of Rishonim and Acharonim that surpasses my knowledge base. So what are this siddur and appendix doing?I am basing myself on my unique area of expertise — the frum teenager. In order to

any issue properly, one needs to be an expert in the reality of the issue. And as far as the reality of teenagers goes, I have merited over the past forty years to have many DMCs (deep and meaningful conversations) with your mainstream “good” frum yeshiva

/Bais Yaakov girls from all over North America, England, and Israel. Many of these DMCs have been in person and many have been by email. And I’m not talking about those who might be termed “messed-up” or “off-the-derech” hanging out on street corners. Those kids are doing fine! They are being honest with where they are holding, and we have invested financial and human resources to create programs to educate them, validate them, embrace them, and thus get them back. I am talking instead about the “good” kids — the “don’t ask, don’t tell,” or the “walk the walk, talk the talk” kids. Those are the ones who are either acting out somewhat (or a lot), but under the radar, or who are not acting out but are simply unexcited — either way, they are full of questions. In every community, in every “style” of education, no matter how sheltered and

or large and metropolitan, no matter “in town” or “out of town” — they are all the same! They’re all asking the same questions and all share the same nagging concerns. And that is fine!As Harav Wolbe,
